claim: The structure of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pol I-CF-DNA was solved to 3.8 Å resolution using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we solve a structure of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pol I-CF-DNA to 3.8 Å resolution using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution achieved and the method used.

claim: Core Factor recognizes the promoter from −27 to −16.
source: The structure reveals a bipartite architecture of Core Factor and its recognition of the promoter from −27 to −16.
evidence: The abstract states the specific promoter region recognized by Core Factor.

claim: Core Factor's intrinsic mobility correlates with different conformational states of the Pol I cleft.
source: Core Factor's intrinsic mobility correlates well with different conformational states of the Pol I cleft, in addition to the stabilization of either Rrn7 N-terminal domain near Pol I wall or the tandem winged helix domain of A49 at a partially overlapping location.
evidence: The abstract describes the correlation between Core Factor mobility and Pol I cleft conformations.

claim: A ratchet motion of the Core Factor-DNA sub-complex at upstream facilitates promoter melting in an ATP-independent manner.
source: Comparison of the three states in this study with the Pol II system suggests that a ratchet motion of the Core Factor-DNA sub-complex at upstream facilitates promoter melting in an ATP-independent manner, distinct from a DNA translocase actively threading the downstream DNA in the Pol II PIC.
evidence: The abstract proposes a mechanism based on comparison with Pol II system.

claim: Pol I transcription accounts for up to 60% of total cellular RNA synthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: The large ribosomal RNA precursor (pre-rRNA) is transcribed by Pol I (Moss et al., 2007), accounting for up to 60% of total cellular RNA synthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Warner, 1999).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference supporting this quantitative claim.

claim: Mis-regulation of Pol I transcription has been implicated in various types of cancer.
source: Transcription by Pol I is highly regulated, and its mis-regulation has been implicated in many diseases including various types of cancer (Drygin et al., 2010; Montanaro et al., 2013; White, 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references linking Pol I mis-regulation to cancer.

claim: Yeast Pol I transcription initiation is regulated by four general transcription factors: Rrn3, Core Factor (CF), TBP, and UAF.
source: Yeast Pol I transcription initiation is regulated by four general transcription factors: the regulatory factor Rrn3, the Core Factor (CF), the TATA-box Binding Protein (TBP), and the Upstream Activation Factor (UAF) (Schneider, 2012).
evidence: The introduction lists the four transcription factors with citation.

claim: Rrn3 contains an elongated HEAT repeat.
source: Rrn3 contains an elongated HEAT repeat (Blattner et al., 2011), and binds Pol I via contacts with subunits A43, A190, and AC40 (Blattner et al., 2011; Cavanaugh et al., 2008; Engel et al., 2016; Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998; Peyroche et al., 2000; Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference describing Rrn3 structure.

claim: Rrn3 binds Pol I via contacts with subunits A43, A190, and AC40.
source: Rrn3 contains an elongated HEAT repeat (Blattner et al., 2011), and binds Pol I via contacts with subunits A43, A190, and AC40 (Blattner et al., 2011; Cavanaugh et al., 2008; Engel et al., 2016; Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998; Peyroche et al., 2000; Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references describing Rrn3-Pol I interactions.

claim: Rrn3 association stabilizes Pol I in its monomeric and initiation-competent form.
source: Rrn3 association stabilizes Pol I in its monomeric and initiation-competent form (Blattner et al., 2011; Engel et al., 2016; Pilsl et al., 2016; Torreira et al., 2017), with which Core Factor further engages to facilitate Pre-Initiation Complex assembly and transcription initiation (Aprikian et al., 2001; Knutson and Hahn, 2013; Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998; Peyroche et al., 2000; Schneider, 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting this functional claim.

claim: Core Factor has been implicated in transcription bubble opening.
source: In addition to recruiting Pol I/Rrn3 to the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) promoter, Core Factor has also been implicated in transcription bubble opening (Kahl et al., 2000).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference supporting Core Factor's role in bubble opening.

claim: Core Factor recruitment to the rDNA promoter in vivo requires the association of UAF with the upstream activating sequence (UAS) and TBP.
source: Core Factor recruitment to the rDNA promoter in vivo requires the association of UAF with the upstream activating sequence (UAS) and TBP (Bordi et al., 2001; Oakes et al., 1999; Steffan et al., 1996; Vannini, 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references describing Core Factor recruitment requirements.

claim: TFIIB binds the Pol II dock and wall domains using its N-terminal zinc ribbon.
source: TFIIB binds the Pol II dock and wall domains using its N-terminal zinc ribbon (ZR) (Bushnell et al., 2004; Chen and Hahn, 2004) and C-terminal cyclin fold domains (Chen and Hahn, 2004; Kostrewa et al., 2009; Sainsbury et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: The introduction cites references describing TFIIB binding to Pol II.

claim: The Rrn7 subunit of Core Factor is predicted to share sequence homology with TFIIB.
source: The Rrn7 subunit of Core Factor is predicted to share sequence homology with TFIIB (Blattner et al., 2011; Knutson and Hahn, 2011; Naidu et al., 2011), containing similar ZR and cyclin fold domains in addition to a helical C-terminal domain (CTD).
evidence: The introduction cites references predicting Rrn7-TFIIB homology.

claim: Rrn6, Rrn7, and Rrn11 are essential subunits of Core Factor.
source: In addition to Rrn7, Rrn6 and Rrn11 are essential subunits of Core Factor (Lalo et al., 1996; Lin et al., 1996).
evidence: The introduction cites references identifying essential Core Factor subunits.

claim: The human ortholog of Core Factor is Selectivity Factor 1 (SL1).
source: The human ortholog of Core Factor is Selectivity Factor 1 (SL1), which comprises three evolutionarily conserved core subunits and two additional metazoan-specific subunits, TAF1D and TAF12 (Denissov et al., 2007; Gorski et al., 2007), suggesting a conserved architecture between these Pol I general transcription factors (Knutson and Hahn, 2013; et al., 2006; Schneider, 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites references describing the human ortholog of Core Factor.

claim: In the atomic structure of Pol I determined by X-ray crystallography, a dimeric configuration and an expanded DNA-binding cleft were observed.
source: First, in the atomic structure of Pol I determined by X-ray crystallography, a dimeric configuration and an expanded DNA-binding cleft were observed (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites references describing the crystal structure of Pol I.

claim: When interacting with Rrn3, both the expander and the connector are displaced, resulting in a monomeric form of Pol I, with a more contracted cleft and a partially rewound bridge helix.
source: When interacting with Rrn3, both the expander and the connector are displaced, resulting in a monomeric form of Pol I, with a more contracted cleft and a partially rewound bridge helix (Engel et al., 2016; Pilsl et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references describing Pol I conformational changes upon Rrn3 binding.

claim: A further contraction of the cleft and a completely folded bridge helix were observed in the elongation form of Pol I revealed by cryo-EM.
source: A further contraction of the cleft and a completely folded bridge helix were observed in the elongation form of Pol I revealed by cryo-EM (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references describing the elongation form of Pol I.

claim: A nucleic acid scaffold containing a 17-nucleotide mismatched transcription bubble in the presence of a 6-nt RNA molecule was used to stabilize the complex.
source: In order to stabilize the complex, we used a nucleic acid scaffold containing a 17-nucleotide (nt) mismatched transcription bubble in the presence of a 6-nt RNA molecule, mimicking an initial transcribing state (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the scaffold design, and Figure 1A shows the scaffold structure.

claim: Single particle analysis using RELION produced a reconstruction with an overall resolution of 3.8 Å.
source: Single particle analysis using RELION (Kimanius et al., 2016; Scheres, 2012) produced a reconstruction with an overall resolution of 3.8 Å (FSC = 0.143 criterion) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: The Results section states the resolution achieved, with supporting figures.

claim: The reconstruction shows a bipartite configuration, with the large module showing clear features of Pol I and the small lobe corresponding to Core Factor.
source: The reconstruction shows a bipartite configuration, with the large module showing clear features of Pol I and the small lobe corresponding to Core Factor.
evidence: The Results section describes the overall architecture of the reconstruction.

claim: DNA density was observed both inside and upstream of the Pol I cleft.
source: DNA density was observed both inside and upstream of the Pol I cleft (Figure 1B), with the upstream DNA interacting with Core Factor.
evidence: The Results section describes DNA density observed in the reconstruction, with Figure 1B showing the density.

claim: The Pol I core region is very rigid with resolution mostly at 3.5 Å, whereas peripheral regions such as the stalk and Core Factor are more mobile with a lower resolution (4.5 to 5.5 Å).
source: Local resolution estimation shows that the Pol I core region is very rigid with resolution mostly at 3.5 Å, whereas peripheral regions such as the stalk and Core Factor are more mobile with a lower resolution (4.5 to 5.5 Å) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The Results section describes local resolution variations, with supporting figure.

claim: Maximum-likelihood based 3D classification revealed that Core Factor adopts different orientations relative to Pol I.
source: Indeed, maximum-likelihood based 3D classification revealed that Core Factor adopts different orientations relative to Pol I, likely suggesting a continuous motion for Core Factor.
evidence: The Results section describes 3D classification results.

claim: Focused refinements on Core Factor and Pol I separately resulted in improved density maps with an overall resolution of 3.7 Å and 4.2 Å, respectively.
source: This resulted in improved density maps for both Pol I and Core Factor, with an overall resolution of 3.7 Å and 4.2 Å, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The Results section describes the focused refinement results, with supporting figures.

claim: Pol I within the Initial Transcribing Complex reconstruction resembles the Elongation Complex more than the apo crystal structure, with a contracted active site cleft.
source: Compared to similar structures determined by either crystallography in the apo form (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013) or cryo-EM in an Elongation Complex (EC) (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016), Pol I within our Initial Transcribing Complex reconstruction resembles the Elongation Complex more than the apo crystal structure, with a contracted active site cleft (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section compares the structure to previous structures, with supporting figure.

claim: Core Factor engages Pol I in the vicinity of the protrusion domain near the upstream entrance of the DNA binding cleft.
source: In addition, Core Factor engages Pol I in the vicinity of the protrusion domain near the upstream entrance of the DNA binding cleft, and intimately interacts with the upstream promoter DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: The Results section describes Core Factor-Pol I interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: Rrn3 and TBP were not observed in the reconstructions.
source: Although we included both Rrn3 and TBP in our assembly reactions (Materials and methods), we did not observe densities in any of the classified reconstructions that could correspond to them (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section states that Rrn3 and TBP were not observed in the reconstructions.

claim: All of the Rrn3 protein was in the unbound and the first wash fractions.
source: Consistent with the absence of Rrn3 in our reconstructions, we found out that all of the Rrn3 protein was in the unbound and the first wash fractions (lanes 5 and 6 in Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Results section describes gel electrophoresis results showing Rrn3 in unbound fractions, with supporting figure.

claim: The overall structure of DNA-bound Core Factor resembles a right hand holding the DNA molecule between the fingers and the palm, with the thumb pointing toward Pol I.
source: The overall structure of DNA-bound Core Factor resembles a right hand holding the DNA molecule between the fingers and the palm, with the thumb pointing toward Pol I (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the overall architecture of Core Factor, with supporting figure.

claim: Rrn6 plays a scaffolding role in the assembly of Core Factor, spanning the palm and the knuckles.
source: Rrn6 plays a scaffolding role in the assembly of Core Factor, spanning the palm and the knuckles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn6's role in Core Factor assembly, with supporting figure.

claim: Rrn6 is composed of an N-terminal domain (NTD), a WD40 repeat domain, a helical bundle (HB) domain, and a C-terminal unstructured region.
source: As predicted (Knutson et al., 2014), Rrn6 is composed of an N-terminal domain (NTD), a WD40 repeat domain, a helical bundle (HB) domain, and a C-terminal unstructured region (Figure 2A).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn6 domain architecture, with supporting figure and citation.

claim: Rrn11 is composed of 13 helices and three long loops.
source: In agreement with the prediction, we can assign most of Rrn11 to helical densities, with a total of 13 helices and three long loops (H2-H3, H4-H5, and H8-H9) (Figures 1B and 2B).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn11 structure, with supporting figures.

claim: Rrn7 contains two cyclin fold domains.
source: Like its counterpart TFIIB in the Pol II system, Rrn7 contains two cyclin fold domains (Knutson and Hahn, 2011; Naidu et al., 2011) (Figure 2C), which form the fingers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn7 domain architecture, with supporting figures and citations.

claim: The two cyclin fold domains of Rrn7 adopt a different relative orientation compared to their counterparts in TFIIB.
source: The two cyclin fold domains can be aligned with those in TFIIB individually (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), but a different relative orientation between them is adopted compared to their counterparts in TFIIB. One of the cyclin fold domains of TFIIB must be rotated when the other is aligned to its counterpart in Rrn7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), to achieve the more compact organization in Rrn7.
evidence: The Results section describes structural comparison between Rrn7 and TFIIB, with supporting figures.

claim: The interaction between Core Factor and Pol I in the Initial Transcribing Complex is mainly mediated by the Rrn11 TPR domain and the Pol I protrusion.
source: The interaction between Core Factor and Pol I in the Initial Transcribing Complex is mainly mediated by the Rrn11 TPR domain (the thumb) and the Pol I protrusion (Figure 2F).
evidence: The Results section describes Core Factor-Pol I interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: The interface between Rrn11 and the Pol I protrusion is rather small, involving Rrn11 helices H8, H10 and H12.
source: Compared to the large interfaces among Core Factor subunits, the interface between Rrn11 and the Pol I protrusion is rather small, involving Rrn11 helices H8, H10 and H12 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The Results section describes the Core Factor-Pol I interface, with supporting figure.

claim: The downstream duplex DNA is inserted into the active site cleft of Pol I, stabilized by interactions with the clamp head, the cleft and the jaw domains of A190, the lobe domain of A135, and Rpb5.
source: The downstream duplex DNA is inserted into the active site cleft of Pol I, stabilized by interactions with the clamp head, the cleft and the jaw domains of A190, the lobe domain of A135, and Rpb5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), similar to Pol II initiation complexes (He et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2015; Plaschka et al., 2016) and Elongation Complexes of all three eukaryotic RNA polymerases (Barnes et al., 2015; Bernecky et al., 2016; Gnatt et al., 2001; Hoffmann et al., 2015; Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section describes downstream DNA interactions, with supporting figure and citations.

claim: A cryo-EM reconstruction of the Pol I/Core Factor complex using a truncated nucleic acid scaffold was obtained at an overall resolution of 6.9 Å.
source: To overcome this, we assembled the Pol I/Core Factor complex using a truncated nucleic acid scaffold (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and obtained a cryo-EM reconstruction at an overall resolution of 6.9 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The Results section describes the truncated scaffold reconstruction, with supporting figures.

claim: Two consecutive kinks of ~35° and ~45° near position −16 that are approximately 5 bp apart are generated by multiple protein-DNA contacts.
source: In contrast, two consecutive kinks of ~35° and ~45° near position −16 that are approximately 5 bp apart are generated by multiple protein-DNA contacts (Figure 3A).
evidence: The Results section describes DNA bending in the Pol I complex, with supporting figure.

claim: Rrn7 mainly uses its N-terminal cyclin fold domain to interact with promoter DNA from positions −27 to −20.
source: Rrn7 mainly uses its N-terminal cyclin fold domain to interact with promoter DNA from positions −27 to −20 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn7-DNA interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: Rrn11 contacts promoter DNA from positions −24 to −16.
source: Rrn11 contacts promoter DNA from positions −24 to −16 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The Results section describes Rrn11-DNA interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: These Core Factor-promoter interfaces agree well with previous photo-crosslinking and Methidiumpropyl-EDTA·Fe(II) footprinting experiments.
source: These Core Factor-promoter interfaces agree well with previous photo-crosslinking (Bric et al., 2004) and Methidiumpropyl-EDTA·Fe(II) footprinting (Bateman and Paule, 1988) experiments.
evidence: The Results section cites previous experiments that support the observed Core Factor-DNA interfaces.

claim: Pol I contacts the upstream DNA near position −10, where the duplex DNA is sandwiched between the wall and the protrusion.
source: Pol I also contacts the upstream DNA near position −10 (Figure 3D). At this location, the duplex DNA is sandwiched between the wall and the protrusion (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section describes Pol I-DNA interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: The upstream promoter DNA is positioned above the Pol II cleft in the Pol II Pre-Initiation Complex.
source: This is distinct from Pol II Pre-Initiation Complex, in which the upstream promoter DNA is positioned above the Pol II cleft (He et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2015; Plaschka et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites references describing Pol II PIC structure for comparison.

claim: When Pol II enters the elongation state, the upstream duplex DNA shifts ~20 Å to the same corresponding location as the upstream DNA in the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex.
source: Interestingly, when Pol II enters the elongation state, the upstream duplex DNA shifts ~20 Å (Barnes et al., 2015; Bernecky et al., 2016) to the same corresponding location as the upstream DNA in the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex.
evidence: The Results section cites references describing Pol II elongation complex for comparison.

claim: Upstream DNA is stabilized by the A135 protrusion domain in Pol I Elongation Complex.
source: This, together with the fact that upstream DNA is also stabilized by the A135 protrusion domain in Pol I Elongation Complex (Tafur et al., 2016), indicates that Pol I initiation complex is pre-conditioned in an elongation-competent state by Core Factor even at the initiation step.
evidence: The Results section cites a reference describing Pol I elongation complex.

claim: Three distinct functional states of the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex were obtained with overall resolutions of 4.2 Å, 4.3 Å and 3.9 Å for states designated State 1, 2, and 3.
source: We thereby subsequently obtained reconstructions of the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex in three distinct functional states (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with overall resolutions of 4.2 Å, 4.3 Å and 3.9 Å for states we respectively designate State 1, 2, and 3.
evidence: The Results section describes the three functional states with their resolutions, with supporting figures.

claim: Core Factor and upstream DNA adopt a range of positions on Pol I, with a rotational movement of up to 10°.
source: Core Factor and upstream DNA adopt a range of positions on Pol I, with a rotational movement of up to 10° (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The Results section describes Core Factor movement, with supporting figures.

claim: In State 2, the movement of Core Factor/DNA correlates with the stabilization of Rrn7 zinc ribbon/linker on Pol I.
source: In State 2, the movement of Core Factor/DNA correlates well with the stabilization of Rrn7 zinc ribbon/linker on Pol I (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Results section describes State 2 features, with supporting figures.

claim: Yeast extracts prepared from the strain lacking the zinc ribbon domain of Rrn7 (ΔZR) failed to support the open complex formation.
source: Indeed, yeast extracts prepared from the strain lacking the zinc ribbon domain of Rrn7 (ΔZR) failed to support the open complex formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental results showing the functional importance of Rrn7 zinc ribbon, with supporting figures.

claim: The recombinant ΔZR Core Factor failed to recover the defect in open complex formation in the ΔZR extract, whereas the wild type complex did.
source: In addition, the recombinant ΔZR Core Factor also failed to recover the defect in open complex formation in the ΔZR extract, whereas the wild type (WT) complex did (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: The Results section describes experimental results showing the functional importance of Rrn7 zinc ribbon, with supporting figures.

claim: In State 3, strong density near the Pol I wall domain and the upstream promoter DNA corresponds to the A49 tandem winged helix (tWH) domain.
source: Intriguingly, in State 3, we observed strong density near the Pol I wall domain and the upstream promoter DNA corresponding to the A49 tandem winged helix (tWH) domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The Results section describes State 3 features, with supporting figure.

claim: There are clear clashes between the Rrn7 linker region and the A49 tandem winged helix domain when comparing State 2 with State 3.
source: Comparison of State 2 with State 3 reveals another striking feature in that there are clear clashes between the Rrn7 linker region and the A49 tandem winged helix domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The Results section describes structural comparison between State 2 and State 3, with supporting figure.

claim: The Pol I clamp gradually closes up to 4 Å from State 1 to State 3.
source: We also discovered a continuous movement of the Pol I clamp, which gradually closes up to 4 Å from State 1 to State 3 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The Results section describes clamp movement across the three states, with supporting figures.

claim: The closing of the clamp correlates with the stabilization of the A49 linker region.
source: Importantly, the closing of the clamp correlates well with the stabilization of the A49 linker region (Figure 4D–F) which likely leads to the stabilization of the tandem winged helix domain.
evidence: The Results section describes correlation between clamp closing and A49 linker stabilization, with supporting figures.

claim: At least three consecutive nucleotides of the non-template DNA at the downstream fork of the transcription bubble is gradually stabilized from State 1 to State 3.
source: In addition, at least three consecutive nucleotides of the non-template DNA at the downstream fork of the transcription bubble is also gradually stabilized (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The Results section describes DNA stabilization across the three states, with supporting figures.

claim: The three functional states of the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex likely represent snapshots of ordered events during transcription initiation: State 1 precedes State 2, which is then followed by State 3.
source: Transcription initiation by Pol I is a dynamic process, and the three functional states of Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex likely represent snapshots of ordered events during transcription initiation: State 1 precedes State 2, which is then followed by State 3.
evidence: The Discussion section proposes a temporal order for the three states.

claim: State 1 with a slightly open cleft should correspond to the step right after the loading of the promoter DNA.
source: First, we observed a gradual closing of the cleft from State 1 to State 3. This is in accordance with the findings that the Pol I cleft is in an open configuration when not bound to DNA as is observed in the apo crystal structures (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013), which contracts upon DNA engagement in Elongation Complex (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016). Thus, State 1 with a slightly open cleft should correspond to the step right after the loading of the promoter DNA, whereas State 3 adopts a more closed cleft resembling the elongation mode.
evidence: The Discussion section proposes the functional significance of State 1 based on cleft conformation, with citations.

claim: State 2 may represent the state of bubble opening, following promoter DNA insertion while preceding initial RNA synthesis.
source: Third, State 2 is an intermediate between State 1 and 3 in terms of clamp closing and tandem winged helix domain stabilization (Figure 4D–F). Additionally, we observed stabilized zinc ribbon and linker regions of Rrn7, in a conformation similar to that of TFIIB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). Moreover, the Rrn7 zinc ribbon domain functions in transcription bubble opening (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). Thus, State 2 may represent the state of bubble opening, following promoter DNA insertion while preceding initial RNA synthesis.
evidence: The Discussion section proposes the functional significance of State 2 based on structural features and functional data, with supporting figures.

claim: State 3 may reflect the initial transcribing state prior to promoter escape.
source: Second, in line with the movement of the clamp, the A49 tandem winged helix domain is only stabilized in State 3, along with the gatekeeper helices in the linker region spanning over the cleft (Figure 4C,F). Given the roles of A49 tandem winged helix domain during transcription elongation (Beckouet et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2010; Pilsl et al., 2016), State 3 may reflect the initial transcribing state prior to promoter escape.
evidence: The Discussion section proposes the functional significance of State 3 based on A49 tWH stabilization, with citations and supporting figures.

claim: The intrinsic mobility of Core Factor may constantly insert the duplex DNA toward the active site by applying a force against Rpb5.
source: Thus, the intrinsic mobility of Core Factor may constantly insert the duplex DNA toward the active site by applying a force against Rpb5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The Discussion section proposes a mechanism for DNA insertion based on Core Factor mobility, with supporting figure.

claim: When Core Factor reaches a critical position, the Rrn7 ZR/linker regions are stabilized on Pol I, likely resulting in spontaneous melting of DNA.
source: When Core Factor reaches a critical position, the Rrn7 ZR/linker regions are stabilized on Pol I. This likely results in a spontaneous melting of DNA that is stabilized by the closing Pol I active site cleft and Rrn7 N-terminal region, followed by the stabilization of the downstream DNA by the clamp head and jaw domains of A190, the lobe domain of A135, and Rpb5, forming a stable open complex (Figure 6B; Video 2).
evidence: The Discussion section proposes a mechanism for DNA melting based on Core Factor positioning, with supporting figure and video.

claim: This model is consistent with the finding that rDNA promoter opening only requires TIF-IB/CF and Pol I in Acanthamoeba castellanii.
source: This model is consistent with the finding that rDNA promoter opening only requires TIF-IB/CF and Pol I in Acanthamoeba castellanii (Kahl et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a reference supporting the proposed mechanism.

claim: The A49 tandem winged helix domain can displace the Rrn7 zinc ribbon/linker to clear the RNA exit channel for subsequent RNA extension.
source: Intriguingly, the A49 tandem winged helix domain can also displace the Rrn7 zinc ribbon/linker to clear the RNA exit channel for subsequent RNA extension (Figures 4B and 6C; Video 2).
evidence: The Discussion section proposes a mechanism for RNA exit channel clearance, with supporting figures and video.

claim: The cyclin fold domains of Rrn7 are located at a more distal position relative to Pol I, different from that of TFIIB.
source: However, the cyclin fold domains of Rrn7 are located at a more distal position relative to Pol I, different from that of TFIIB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Discussion section compares Rrn7 and TFIIB positioning, with supporting figure.

claim: The cyclin fold domains of Rrn7 are mainly involved in promoter DNA interaction, lacking an essential interface with the polymerase compared to TFIIB.
source: Consistent with this, the cyclin fold domains of Rrn7 are mainly involved in promoter DNA interaction (Figure 3), lacking an essential interface with the polymerase compared to TFIIB.
evidence: The Discussion section describes functional differences between Rrn7 and TFIIB, with supporting figure.

claim: The N-terminal cyclin fold domain in TFIIB specifically recognizes the downstream BRE (TFIIB recognition element), forcing the DNA to take a completely different path.
source: In addition, the N-terminal cyclin fold domain in TFIIB specifically recognizes the downstream BRE (TFIIB recognition element), forcing the DNA to take a completely different path (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Discussion section describes TFIIB-DNA interaction, with supporting figure.

claim: The upstream promoter DNA in Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex and Elongation Complex occupy a very similar location on Pol I by contacting both the wall and the protrusion.
source: Second, the upstream promoter DNA in Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex and Elongation Complex occupy a very similar location on Pol I by contacting both the wall and the protrusion (Figure 5A), implying that Pol I is pre-conditioned in an elongation-competent form at the initiation stage.
evidence: The Discussion section compares DNA positioning between Pol I ITC and EC, with supporting figure.

claim: The positioning of the upstream promoter DNA in the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex is fundamentally different from that in the Pol II Pre-Initiation Complex.
source: The positioning of the upstream promoter DNA in the Pol I Initial Transcribing Complex is fundamentally different from that in the Pol II Pre-Initiation Complex (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The Discussion section compares DNA positioning between Pol I and Pol II complexes, with supporting figures.

claim: Transition from initiation to elongation for Pol II requires the ATP-dependent translocase activity of TFIIH to insert DNA from downstream into the active site cleft.
source: Transition from initiation to elongation for Pol II requires the ATP-dependent translocase activity of TFIIH to insert DNA from downstream into the active site cleft (Fishburn et al., 2015; Grünberg et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion section cites references describing Pol II transition mechanism.

claim: TFIIH is not required for Pol I transcription initiation.
source: However, TFIIH is not required for Pol I transcription initiation (Assfalg et al., 2012), and no ATP hydrolysis activity has been associated with Pol I general transcription complexes (Lofquist et al., 1993).
evidence: The Discussion section cites references describing Pol I initiation requirements.

claim: No ATP hydrolysis activity has been associated with Pol I general transcription complexes.
source: However, TFIIH is not required for Pol I transcription initiation (Assfalg et al., 2012), and no ATP hydrolysis activity has been associated with Pol I general transcription complexes (Lofquist et al., 1993).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a reference describing Pol I biochemical properties.

claim: Cryo-EM density maps have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) under accession numbers EMD-8771 (full), EMD-8772 (Core Factor, local), EMD-8773 (Pol I, local), EMD-8774 (State 1), EMD-8775 (State 2), EMD-8776 (State 3), EMD-8777 (truncated construct).
source: Cryo-EM density maps have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) under accession numbers EMD-8771 (full), EMD-8772 (Core Factor, local), EMD-8773 (Pol I, local), EMD-8774 (State 1), EMD-8775 (State 2), EMD-8776 (State 3), EMD-8777 (truncated construct).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides data deposition information.

claim: Model coordinates have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession numbers 5W5Y (full), 5W64 (State 1), 5W65 (State 2), 5W66 (State 3).
source: Model coordinates have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession numbers 5W5Y (full), 5W64 (State 1), 5W65 (State 2), 5W66 (State 3).
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides data deposition information.
